text:
The car belonged to the residency, and it came with a laminated sheet of instructions that Ruth had read aloud at the gate like a flight attendant. Do not ride the clutch. Do not trust the fuel gauge. If the check-engine light comes on, it has already been on. Anton took the wheel because he was the only one who had driven a manual in the last decade, and he drove the way he did everything at Ballycarra, with a kind of apologetic competence, as though expecting to be corrected.

"We're going the wrong way," Marian said, around the fourth roundabout.

"The phone says right."

"The phone thinks the sea is a road."

He laughed, and she watched the side of his face do it. In five weeks she had learned a number of things about that face: that it flushed at the ears when he was praised, that it went slack and ten years older when he read his own pages over lunch, that it had a small scar at the chin from a bicycle. She had learned them the way one learns a house one is only renting, by walking through it at night without turning on the lights.

It was the last Saturday. On Monday a van would take her to the airport in Shannon, and on Tuesday Anton would be driven there by the same man, Declan, who talked about hurling. They had discussed this with great cheerfulness, as a joke about logistics. Neither had proposed sharing the van.

The beach was Anton's idea. For five weeks they had looked at the Atlantic from the studio windows and never once gone down to it. "It would be absurd," he'd said on Thursday, "to leave without touching it." Marian had said she was not sure the sea was a thing one touched. But she had packed a bag.

They found a beach eventually, at the end of a lane with grass growing up the middle. A sign in Irish and English asked them to close the gate. Anton parked beside a single tractor and turned off the engine, and the car ticked in the quiet.

"Well," he said.

"Well."

They walked down through the marram grass with the bag between them, each holding one strap, an arrangement that had begun as a courtesy and become awkward without either of them being able to say when. Far off, a man threw something for a dog, and threw it again.

"I brought eggs," Marian said, when they had settled behind a low wall of rock. "And bread. And that cheese Declan swore was local."

"I brought wine."

"Good."

"And no way to open it."

She looked at him. He held up the bottle, a handsome green thing with a real cork, and she saw he was about to be ashamed, and wanted to forestall it, and found, to her irritation, that she was also enjoying it.

"You carried that up here."

"I had a plan. It was a short plan." He was already unlacing a boot. She watched him wrap the bottle in his sweater, press its base into the heel, and strike the boot against the rock again and again with the bent-necked concentration of a man defusing something. The cork rose by degrees. On the ninth blow the bottle slipped, rolled, and landed in the sand, unbroken. They both stared at it.

"That's the second-best outcome," Anton said.

"What's the first?"

"That it worked."

They drank from the two enamel mugs she'd taken from the kitchen, which tasted faintly of tea. It occurred to her that this was precisely the afternoon one is supposed to have at the end of a residency, and that she was having it with the correct person, and that the correctness of it was exactly what made her want to pick at it.

"Do you think," she said, "we'll write to each other?"

He didn't answer at once. He peeled an egg with a thoroughness she found almost unbearable. "I think we'll mean to."

"That's honest."

"It's the only kind I'm good for after a bottle of wine." He glanced at her, then away. "I'd like to. Mean to, I mean. I'd like to mean to for a long time."

It was as near as either of them had come. Three weeks earlier, on the night of the power cut, she had stood in his doorway holding a candle in a jar, and he had said, "I have a torch," and she had said, "I know," and that had been the whole of the discussion. In the morning he had made the porridge. Since then there had been only a gentleness between them, so carefully maintained it had begun to feel like a third resident. He had a wife in Rotterdam, a fact he had mentioned once, early, as one mentions an allergy.

"Let's walk," Marian said. "Before we're too comfortable."

They left the bag in the lee of the rocks and went down toward the water, shoes in hand. Beyond a headland she could see a second strand, smaller, empty, a pure curve of white.

"There," Anton said. "That's the real one. This one was practice."

They went around the point by way of a shelf of black rock, slick with weed, where he gave her his hand twice and she took it twice and neither remarked on it. The second beach was lovelier. Anton wandered down to the waterline while she crouched over shells. When she glanced up he was standing with his trousers rolled to the knee and his arms held slightly out from his sides, a man being introduced to a large animal.

"Cold?" she called.

"Deeply."

"Is it touching you back?"

"I'd say it's taking notes."

She laughed, and some bird lifted off the rocks at the sound. She thought: I will remember this exactly. And she thought, in the same instant, that to think such a thing was already to begin leaving.

It was she who noticed the water. When she stood up, the sand between herself and the point was gone. Not covered, exactly. Shining, shallow, moving. A thin bright current ran through the shelf of rock they'd crossed, and as she watched it lifted a rope of weed and laid it down a foot farther in.

"Anton."

He turned, saw, and said a short word in Dutch.

"How long did we—"

"An hour." He was already walking toward her. "It's fine. It's a few inches."

It was a few inches at the first rock and a good deal more at the second. The water came to her thighs at the lowest point, shockingly cold, and she cried out, and Anton, ahead of her, turned and took her whole forearm in his hand and did not let go until they were up on the dry sand of the first beach, where the man with the dog regarded them with polite and total indifference.

They stood gasping. Anton's trousers, rolled so carefully, were soaked to the belt.

"Well," he said. "We touched it."

"I think it's fair to say it touched us."

The bag was where they had left it, and the wine, miraculously, was upright, and she began to shake with cold and laughter. He took off his sweater, sandy and smelling of the cork, and put it around her shoulders without comment. For a moment his hands stayed at the collar. His face was very near, and she saw the scar at the chin, and the flush climbing his ears, and the question in it, put plainly for once.

She could have said yes. She was almost sure of that, later, in the car, with the heater roaring and their wet hems steaming against the seats. It would have been a clean and decent ending to a story they'd both been careful not to tell. But the dog came bounding up with a stick, and the man was calling, and the moment lifted and settled elsewhere, as a bird does. Anton stepped back and bent to pick up the mugs.

"We should get the car back before Ruth sends a search party."

"She'd send a laminated sheet."

The Fiat started on the third try. He drove with great care, ten and two, and she looked out at the fields going blue in the late light, each divided from the next by a stone wall someone had built by hand a very long time ago. Neither of them spoke. The silence had the quality of a held breath, or of a room in which the furniture has already been covered.

At the roundabout where they had gone wrong that morning, he took the correct exit without consulting the phone.

"You know it now," she said.

"Just in time."

At dinner there would be the others, and a toast, probably, and someone would say it had been such a special month. Marian would agree. Later she would pack, folding the damp skirt into a plastic bag, and find in its pocket three shells, which she would hold for a minute in her palm and then, instead of throwing away, wrap in a sock.

But that was still ahead. For now there was the road, and the heater, and Anton's hand on the gearshift, which had not moved in some time and which she did not look at. Somewhere behind them the tide was coming all the way in, covering the second beach, the rocks, the shining place where they had stood, and in the morning there would be no sign.

"Marian," he said.

"Yes."

"Nothing. I just wanted to say it."

"All right," she said. "Say it again."

He did, at the next turning, and then they were home.
